sections.title: An iron pillar that will not rust
sections.intro_md:
In the courtyard of a ruined mosque in south Delhi stands a dark metal column about **7.2 metres** tall. It was cast around **400 CE**, in the time of the Gupta kings, probably for a temple far from here, and it has stood in the open air for well over a thousand years. It has barely rusted.

Nobody in the 4th century wrote down how they made it. Metallurgists only worked out the answer in the 1990s and 2000s. Beside it rises the **Qutb Minar**, a fluted tower of red sandstone begun in about **1199** by the first Turkish sultan of Delhi, built partly from the stones of 27 temples he had pulled down. The pillar was already some 800 years old when the tower began.

That pairing is Delhi in one courtyard. Ancient Indian craft, a conquest, recycled stone, an inscription in Sanskrit next to one in Arabic, and a crowd of schoolchildren taking selfies in front of both. Few cities have been a capital as many times, or been destroyed as many times, and kept every layer visible.

spotlights.name: The Iron Pillar
spotlights.when: Cast about 400 CE; moved to Delhi by about the 11th century
spotlights.spot_it: A dark, smooth metal column about 7 m tall inside a railing, in a courtyard of broken sandstone arches.
spotlights.story_md: The pillar weighs more than **6 tonnes** and is made of about **98% wrought iron**, hammered together from many smaller pieces. A Sanskrit inscription names a king called Chandra, usually taken to be **Chandragupta II**. Its secret is phosphorus: the iron holds unusually high phosphorus and almost no sulphur, so a thin protective film of a compound called **misawite** forms on the surface and stops rust from going deep. Delhi's dry climate helps. A popular custom said that anyone who could circle it with their arms behind their back would have a wish granted; the Archaeological Survey fenced it off in **1997** because the hugging was wearing it down.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is proof that Indian smiths were making corrosion-resistant iron 1,600 years ago.
spotlights.memory_hook: Sixteen centuries in the open, and the rust gave up first.

spotlights.name: Qutb Minar
spotlights.spot_it: A tall, fluted brick-and-sandstone tower that tapers in five storeys, each ringed by a carved balcony.
spotlights.story_md: At **72.5 metres**, the Qutb Minar is one of the tallest brick minarets in the world. **Qutb ud-Din Aibak** built the first storey; his successor **Iltutmish** added three more. Lightning knocked off the top in 1369 and **Firoz Shah Tughlaq** rebuilt it with white marble, which is why the upper storeys look different. The bands of carving mix Quranic verses with lotus and bell motifs that Hindu masons carved from habit. Visitors could climb the **379 steps** until **4 December 1981**, when a power cut and a stampede on the stairs killed 45 people, many of them schoolchildren. It has been closed to climbers since.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It announced a new kind of ruler in north India, and it is still Delhi's oldest landmark.
spotlights.memory_hook: Five storeys, three builders, one lightning strike.

sections.title: The capital at a glance
sections.intro_md:
Delhi is not a state and not quite a union territory. Since **1991**, under the 69th amendment, it has been the **National Capital Territory**: it elects a 70-member assembly and a chief minister, but police, public order and land answer to the Union government through the **Lieutenant Governor**. That split explains a decade of court fights between Delhi's elected government and the LG.

The territory covers just **1,484 km²**, smaller than many Indian districts. In 2011 it held **16.8 million** people, giving it a density of about **11,300 per km²**, the highest of any state or territory. Estimates now put the territory above **22 million**, and the wider National Capital Region, spilling into Haryana, Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan, already held about **46 million** in 2011. New Delhi, the planned capital inside it, is only one small part.

The money is just as concentrated. Delhi's per capita income was an estimated **₹5,31,610** in 2025 to 26, about **2.5 times** the Indian average, and services make up **86%** of its economy. Since December 2025 it has been divided into **13 districts**, up from 11.

spotlights.name: India Gate
spotlights.spot_it: A 42 m sandstone arch at the end of a long lawn-lined avenue, a flame or a canopy nearby, crowds and ice-cream carts at dusk.
spotlights.story_md: India Gate was designed by **Edwin Lutyens** as the All India War Memorial. Carved on its stone are the names of about **13,300** Indian and British soldiers of the British Indian Army who died between 1914 and 1921, in the First World War and the Third Anglo-Afghan War. The Amar Jawan Jyoti, an eternal flame for the soldiers of the 1971 war, burned under the arch from 1972 until **January 2022**, when it was merged with the flame at the new **National War Memorial** next door. The empty canopy behind the arch once held a statue of George V; since **2022** it holds a statue of **Subhas Chandra Bose**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the capital's front lawn, where Delhi goes to be seen on a winter evening.
spotlights.memory_hook: A colonial war memorial that now shelters Netaji.

spotlights.name: The Yamuna in Delhi
spotlights.when: The river that made every Delhi possible
spotlights.spot_it: A wide, slow, grey-green river with a broad floodplain of fields and scrub, crossed by iron rail bridges and new cable-stayed spans.
spotlights.story_md: Every Delhi was built between the **Aravalli ridge** and the **Yamuna**: rock for defence, river for water. The river runs about **22 km** through the territory, from the Wazirabad barrage to Okhla, which is about **2%** of its length. Yet official reports estimate that this stretch contributes roughly **three-quarters** of the river's total pollution load, because untreated sewage from big drains like Najafgarh pours in. In July 2023 the river rose to **208.66 m** at the Old Railway Bridge, its highest on record, and flooded the Red Fort's outer road and the area around the Supreme Court.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Delhi drinks from this river and drains into it, often on the same day.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two per cent of the river, three-quarters of the dirt.

sections.title: Rock, river and birds of prey
sections.intro_md:
Delhi sits on a plain, but its bones are the **Delhi Ridge**, the last worn-down tail of the **Aravalli** range, among the oldest fold mountains on Earth. The ridge runs in a rough arc from the southern border to the river near Wazirabad. Older Delhis clung to it; Tughlaqabad and Mehrauli sit on its rock.

The climate is harsh at both ends. May and June bring dust storms and afternoon temperatures above **45°C**; on **29 May 2024** the city's official station at Safdarjung recorded 46.8°C while other sensors reported higher readings that were later questioned. In December and January, cold fog grounds flights and nights fall to about **3 to 5°C**. The monsoon delivers most of the year's roughly **750 mm** of rain in July and August.

For a megacity, Delhi is unusually wild. About a fifth of its area is under green cover. It has leopards in the southern ridge, nilgai on the golf courses, rhesus macaques in the government buildings, and one of the densest populations of large birds of prey of any city in the world.

spotlights.name: The Delhi Ridge

where.label: Central Ridge near Buddha Jayanti Park

spotlights.when: Rock more than a billion years old
spotlights.spot_it: Low rocky hills of grey quartzite covered in thorny scrub and the umbrella-shaped invasive vilayati kikar.
spotlights.story_md: The ridge is the city's **green lung** and its rainwater sponge, and it is split into four protected blocks: Northern, Central, South Central and Southern. Much of it is now covered by **vilayati kikar** (*Prosopis juliflora*), a Mexican thorn tree the British planted in the 1910s to green the rocks. It worked too well, smothering native trees like dhak and kair. Since the 2010s, the Delhi forest department and the Delhi Development Authority have been cutting it back and replanting native species in parks like **Aravalli Biodiversity Park**. The northern ridge also holds memorials of the 1857 siege, when British troops camped on its rocks.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Without the ridge Delhi would be hotter, drier and much harder to defend.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ancient rock, a Mexican tree, a war camp.

spotlights.name: Black kites

where.label: Across the city, densest near Old Delhi

spotlights.when: Year-round residents, peak breeding in monsoon
spotlights.spot_it: Brown hawks with a forked tail circling in dozens over markets and rooftops, whistling a thin, shivering call.
spotlights.story_md: Delhi may hold one of the **highest densities of large raptors of any city** in the world, mostly black kites. Researchers have found that the birds thrive because people feed them: in Old Delhi, Muslim families toss scraps of meat into the air as an act of charity, a practice tied to ideas of warding off misfortune. The kites also scavenge at slaughterhouses and dumps. The brothers **Nadeem and Saud Shehzad** have rescued thousands of injured kites from manja kite strings in a basement in Wazirabad, the subject of the 2022 documentary **All That Breathes**, which won the documentary prize at Cannes and was nominated for an Oscar.
spotlights.why_it_matters: They are Delhi's unofficial city bird, kept alive by kindness and garbage.
spotlights.memory_hook: Meat thrown skyward, kites that never leave.

sections.title: Before the sultans
sections.intro_md:
Delhi likes to say it has had **seven cities**, sometimes eight, sometimes eleven or more, depending on who is counting. The count usually starts with **Lal Kot**, the Tomar Rajputs' fort of the 11th century, and runs through Siri, Tughlaqabad, Jahanpanah, Firozabad, Dinpanah and Shahjahanabad to New Delhi. But people lived here long before.

Legend says the Pandavas of the **Mahabharata** built **Indraprastha** on the Yamuna bank, and many identify it with the mound under the **Purana Qila**. Excavations there have found **Painted Grey Ware** pottery, usually dated to about 1200 to 600 BCE, and an unbroken sequence of occupation from the Mauryan period on. In 1966, a rock in a residential colony near Srinivaspuri was found to carry a minor edict of **Ashoka**, proof that the region mattered in the 3rd century BCE.

The name itself is unexplained. Theories link 'Dilli' to a king named Dhillu, to the Hindi *dehali* (threshold) or to the *dhili* (loose) foundation of the iron pillar. None is proven.

spotlights.name: Purana Qila
spotlights.when: Walls 1530s to 1540s; settlement layers from about 1000 BCE
spotlights.spot_it: Massive grey stone walls and a tall gateway with tiled domed pavilions on top, a boating lake in the old moat below.
spotlights.story_md: The walls belong to **Humayun's** city of **Dinpanah** and to **Sher Shah Suri**, the Afghan who chased him out in 1540 and kept building. Inside stands Sher Shah's elegant mosque and the **Sher Mandal**, an octagonal tower that Humayun, back on the throne, used as a library. In **1556** he slipped on its steep stairs when he heard the call to prayer and died of his injuries two days later. Below, the Archaeological Survey has dug through layers going back to the Painted Grey Ware period, with finds from the Mauryan, Shunga, Kushan, Gupta and Rajput eras, which is why the site keeps coming up in arguments about Indraprastha.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It holds nearly every period of Delhi's past in one mound.
spotlights.memory_hook: An emperor fell down his own library stairs here.

spotlights.name: Ashoka's pillar at Feroz Shah Kotla
spotlights.when: Pillar 3rd century BCE; moved to Delhi 1356
spotlights.spot_it: A smooth, honey-coloured stone shaft rising from the top of a stepped, ruined pyramid of rubble.
spotlights.story_md: **Firoz Shah Tughlaq** liked antiquities. In **1356** he had a 13 m Ashokan pillar moved about **200 km** from Topra, in today's Haryana, to his new city of Firozabad. A chronicler describes it wrapped in cotton and silk, lowered onto a cart with **42 wheels** pulled by thousands of men, then floated down the Yamuna on boats. Nobody at court could read its Brahmi script. It was finally deciphered by **James Prinsep** in **1837**. Every Thursday, people still leave letters to the djinns believed to live in the ruins of Feroz Shah Kotla, asking for jobs, cures and love.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It carries Ashoka's edicts and a medieval king's taste for collecting in the same stone.
spotlights.memory_hook: A sultan moved a pillar he could not read, and people still post letters to djinns beside it.

sections.title: The sultans' Delhi
sections.intro_md:
In **1192** Muhammad of Ghor defeated **Prithviraj Chauhan** at the second battle of Tarain, and his general **Qutb ud-Din Aibak** took Delhi. In 1206 Aibak declared himself sultan. For the next 320 years, five dynasties ruled from here: the **Mamluks** (slave kings), the **Khaljis**, the **Tughlaqs**, the **Sayyids** and the **Lodis**.

They built constantly. The Delhi Sultanate turned back repeated **Mongol** invasions that had flattened Baghdad and much of Persia, which made Delhi a refuge for poets, scholars and Sufis from across the Islamic world. Out of that mix came new architecture, the true arch and dome, and a new language of the street that would become Hindustani.

It also produced India's only woman to sit on the throne of Delhi, a sultan who moved his whole capital and then moved it back, and a ruler who built a reservoir big enough to water a city. Most of what remains is in south Delhi, where tombs stand in parks, between apartment blocks and inside a golf course.

spotlights.name: Alai Darwaza
spotlights.spot_it: A squat, square red sandstone gatehouse inlaid with white marble bands, with horseshoe-shaped pointed arches and a low dome.
spotlights.story_md: Built by **Alauddin Khalji** in **1311** as a gate to the Qutb mosque, the Alai Darwaza is often called the first building in India with **true arches and a true dome**, made with radiating voussoirs rather than stacked, overhanging stones. Its craftsmen probably came from Seljuk Turkey and Persia, refugees from the Mongols. Alauddin himself was ruthless and inventive: he fixed grain prices in Delhi by decree, kept a spy network in the markets, and began a second minar meant to be twice the height of the Qutb. The **Alai Minar** stalled at about 25 m when he died in 1316.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It brought a new engineering idea to India that every later dome relies on.
spotlights.memory_hook: The first true dome, and next door, the stump of a tower that was meant to be twice the Qutb.

spotlights.name: Razia Sultan

where.label: Tomb at Bulbuli Khana, Old Delhi

spotlights.spot_it: A small, roofless, walled grave in a narrow Old Delhi lane, two plain platforms open to the sky.
spotlights.story_md: **Razia**, daughter of Iltutmish, is the only woman to have ruled the Delhi Sultanate. Her father named her heir over his sons. She took the throne in **1236**, dropped the veil, wore a tunic and turban, rode at the head of her army and held open court. Turkish nobles resented her, and chroniclers hint they were especially angry at her closeness to **Jamal-ud-Din Yaqut**, an Abyssinian officer she promoted. She was overthrown in 1240 and killed soon after. Where she is buried is disputed: a modest grave in **Bulbuli Khana** near Turkman Gate is the most cited site, and towns in Haryana and Rajasthan also claim her.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Delhi had a woman ruler seven centuries before it had a woman chief minister.
spotlights.memory_hook: Turban on, veil off, four years on the throne.

spotlights.name: Tughlaqabad Fort
spotlights.spot_it: Miles of sloping, tumbled grey rubble walls with round bastions on a rocky rise, goats grazing in the ruins.
spotlights.story_md: **Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq** built this colossal fortress city in about four years, with walls running some **6.5 km**. Legend says he forced the workers of the Sufi saint **Nizamuddin Auliya** to work on his walls instead of the saint's step-well, and the saint cursed the city: *'Ya rahe ujar, ya base Gujar'*, may it stay desolate or be home to herders. It was abandoned soon after his death in 1325. His son **Muhammad bin Tughlaq** later ordered much of Delhi's population to move to **Daulatabad**, about 1,100 km south, in 1327, then let them return.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the most dramatic ruin in Delhi, and a story about power losing to a saint.
spotlights.memory_hook: Desolate or herders: the curse came true.

spotlights.name: Hazrat Nizamuddin Dargah
spotlights.spot_it: A small marble shrine with a green-and-white dome, glowing with lamps, surrounded by rose-petal sellers and a courtyard packed for evening qawwali.
spotlights.story_md: **Nizamuddin Auliya** (1238 to 1325) was a saint of the **Chishti** Sufi order who preached love, refused gifts from sultans and fed the poor from an open kitchen. His tomb, in a dense medieval lane called the **Basti**, draws people of every faith. On Thursday evenings and on festival nights, hereditary qawwals of the Nizami family sing in the courtyard, a tradition said to run unbroken for about **700 years**. His followers lie around him: the poet **Amir Khusrau**, the Mughal princess **Jahanara**, and the poet Mirza Ghalib a short walk away. The saint is said to have told a hostile sultan, *'Dilli abhi door hai'*: Delhi is still far. The sultan died before reaching it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the spiritual heart of Delhi's composite culture.
spotlights.memory_hook: Rose petals, a green dome, and songs on a Thursday night.

spotlights.name: Amir Khusrau
spotlights.spot_it: Look for his tomb, a marble enclosure with fine jali screens, steps from his master's.
spotlights.story_md: Poet, musician and courtier to at least six sultans, **Amir Khusrau** is called the 'parrot of India'. He wrote in Persian and in **Hindavi**, the spoken language of Delhi, and he is credited, by tradition, with inventing **qawwali**, the **tarana**, and even the sitar and tabla. Musicologists doubt the instruments, but the songs are real: *'Chhap tilak sab chheeni'* and *'Aaj rang hai'* are still sung at the dargah. He was devoted to Nizamuddin, and when the saint died in 1325 Khusrau died within six months. He was buried at his master's feet, and by custom pilgrims visit his tomb first.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He blended Persian and Indian music and language into something new.
spotlights.memory_hook: The parrot of India sings at his master's feet.

spotlights.name: Lodhi Garden
spotlights.spot_it: Domed stone tombs rising from neat lawns and palms, with joggers, yoga groups and couples on benches.
spotlights.story_md: The park holds tombs of the last two sultan dynasties: **Muhammad Shah** of the Sayyids (1444), the domed **Bara Gumbad**, the **Shisha Gumbad** that once glittered with blue glazed tiles, and **Sikandar Lodi's** walled tomb (1517). A village stood among them until the British cleared it in **1936** and laid out 'Lady Willingdon Park', named after the Viceroy's wife. It was renamed after Independence. Today it is the most fashionable morning walk in Delhi, where retired officials, diplomats, dog walkers and laughing clubs share 37 hectares of lawns with 500-year-old ruins.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Delhi lives inside its monuments rather than behind fences.
spotlights.memory_hook: A sultan's tomb, a laughing club, the same lawn.

sections.title: The Mughal city
sections.intro_md:
**Babur** won Delhi at Panipat in **1526**, but the early Mughals preferred Agra and Lahore. Delhi's great Mughal moment came when **Shah Jahan** moved the capital here and built a new walled city, **Shahjahanabad**, between **1639 and 1648**. Its spine was a broad avenue with a canal running down the middle, **Chandni Chowk**, ending at the walls of the **Red Fort**. Its anchor was the **Jama Masjid**, then the largest mosque in India.

At its peak in the late 17th century, Shahjahanabad was one of the richest cities on Earth, with perhaps **400,000** people. Then the empire weakened. In **1739** the Persian ruler **Nadir Shah** sacked it, killed tens of thousands in a single day and carried off the **Peacock Throne** and, by most accounts, the **Koh-i-Noor**. Afghans and Marathas raided in turn, and from **1803** the Mughal emperor lived as a pensioner of the East India Company.

The last act came in **1857**, when rebel sepoys rode in from Meerut and proclaimed the old emperor their leader. The British retook the city after a four-month siege and took a terrible revenge.

Among the densest areas in India

spotlights.name: Humayun's Tomb
spotlights.spot_it: A red sandstone and white marble mausoleum with a swelling white double dome, standing on a high arcaded platform in a garden of channels.
spotlights.story_md: Commissioned by Humayun's widow, **Bega Begum**, and designed by the Persian architect **Mirak Mirza Ghiyas**, this is the **first garden tomb** on the subcontinent and the direct ancestor of the Taj Mahal, built some 70 years later. It sits in a **charbagh**, a garden quartered by water channels, symbolising paradise. More than **150 members** of the Mughal family are buried in its chambers, which earned it the name 'dormitory of the Mughals'. In 1857 the last emperor, **Bahadur Shah Zafar**, took refuge here and was arrested in the grounds. A restoration by the **Aga Khan Trust for Culture** from 1997 brought the water back to its channels.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It set the template for the greatest Mughal buildings, including the Taj.
spotlights.memory_hook: Before the Taj, there was the dormitory of the Mughals.

spotlights.name: Red Fort (Lal Qila)
spotlights.spot_it: Long walls of red sandstone with domed kiosks over the Lahori Gate, a tricolour flying above, and white marble halls inside.
spotlights.story_md: Shah Jahan's palace-fortress was called **Qila-e-Mubarak**, the blessed fort. Its walls run about **2.4 km**. Inside, the **Diwan-i-Khas**, the hall of private audience, once held the Peacock Throne and still carries a Persian couplet often translated as *'If there is paradise on earth, it is this, it is this, it is this.'* The British turned much of the palace into barracks after 1857. On **15 August 1947** Nehru raised the flag at the Lahori Gate, and every prime minister has spoken from its ramparts on Independence Day since. UNESCO listed it in **2007**. In **November 2025** a car bomb near the Red Fort metro station killed at least 11 people.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is where Mughal power peaked and where India announces itself every 15 August.
spotlights.memory_hook: Paradise on earth, then a barracks, then the nation's podium.

spotlights.name: Jama Masjid
spotlights.spot_it: Three bulbous white marble domes with black stripes, two tall striped minarets and a vast raised courtyard reached by broad flights of steps.
spotlights.story_md: Shah Jahan's congregational mosque, properly **Masjid-i-Jahan-Numa**, took **5,000 workers** six years. Its courtyard can hold about **25,000** worshippers. The eastern steps once led to the Red Fort; the southern ones now spill into a market of kebab stalls. After 1857 the British occupied it as barracks and considered demolishing it; it was returned to Muslims in 1862. On Eid, the courtyard fills to its edges. The south minaret can be climbed for a view over Old Delhi's rooftops, a maze of satellite dishes, pigeon lofts and kite strings.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the soul of Old Delhi's Muslim life and its best view.
spotlights.memory_hook: Twenty-five thousand people kneeling in one courtyard.

spotlights.name: Chandni Chowk
spotlights.spot_it: A dense bazaar street under a cobweb of wires, cycle rickshaws, porters with sacks on their heads, temple bells and a gurdwara dome.
spotlights.story_md: The avenue was designed by Shah Jahan's daughter **Jahanara**. A canal once ran down its centre and pooled in a square where moonlight reflected in the water, which is one explanation of the name 'moonlit square'. Today, within a kilometre, stand the Jain **Lal Mandir**, the **Gauri Shankar** temple, **Gurdwara Sis Ganj** where the ninth Sikh Guru, **Tegh Bahadur**, was executed in 1675, the **Sunehri Masjid** and a Baptist church of 1814. A redevelopment completed in **2021** pedestrianised the main stretch in the daytime and buried some of the wires.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a 370-year-old shopping street that still works.
spotlights.memory_hook: Moonlight once floated in its canal; now it is lit by wedding bulbs.

spotlights.name: Mirza Ghalib

where.label: Gali Qasim Jan, Ballimaran, Old Delhi

spotlights.spot_it: A gaunt man in a tall cap and long coat in the one surviving photograph; his old house is a small museum in an alley off Ballimaran.
spotlights.story_md: **Mirza Asadullah Khan Ghalib** is the most quoted poet in Urdu and the last great poet of the Mughal court. He drank, gambled, was jailed briefly for running a gaming house, and complained endlessly about his pension, all in prose so witty that his letters are still read for pleasure. He lived through 1857 and wrote a diary of the siege, *Dastambu*, and letters describing a city emptied by British reprisals. Lines like *'Hazaron khwahishen aisi ki har khwahish pe dam nikle'* (a thousand desires, each worth dying for) are still quoted in Hindi films, WhatsApp forwards and parliamentary debates.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He gave Delhi its voice in its darkest decade.
spotlights.memory_hook: A thousand desires, one pension, endless complaint, perfect verse.

spotlights.name: Bahadur Shah Zafar

where.label: Red Fort to exile in Rangoon

spotlights.spot_it: An old man with a white beard propped on cushions, in the only photograph of him, taken in 1858 after his capture.
spotlights.story_md: The last Mughal emperor was a poet and calligrapher in his 80s who ruled little beyond the Red Fort. In **May 1857** rebel sepoys proclaimed him emperor of Hindustan, and for four months Delhi was the rebellion's capital. When the British stormed back in **September 1857**, he fled to Humayun's Tomb and surrendered. Officer **William Hodson** shot three of the princes dead near a gate still called **Khooni Darwaza**, the bloody gate. Zafar was tried, exiled to **Rangoon** in Burma, and died there in **1862**, buried in an unmarked grave that was only rediscovered in **1991**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: With him, 331 years of Mughal rule ended.
spotlights.memory_hook: The last emperor could not get two yards of Delhi soil.

sections.title: An imperial capital on Raisina Hill
sections.intro_md:
On **12 December 1911**, at the **Delhi Durbar**, King George V announced that the capital of British India would move from Calcutta to Delhi. The reasons were partly political, to escape Bengal's nationalist politics after the 1905 partition, and partly symbolic: Delhi was where emperors had ruled.

The architects **Edwin Lutyens** and **Herbert Baker** planned a new city south of Shahjahanabad, centred on **Raisina Hill**. It took twenty years, a world war and some 30,000 workers. **New Delhi** was inaugurated on **13 February 1931**. Its plan is a web of hexagons and roundabouts, wide avenues lined with neem, jamun and arjun trees, and white bungalows on big plots for officials. Sixteen years later the British left.

Since 2019 the **Central Vista Redevelopment** has rebuilt much of the core: a new triangular **Parliament** opened in **May 2023**, the ceremonial avenue Rajpath was relandscaped and renamed **Kartavya Path** in 2022, and the old North and South Blocks are being turned into a national museum.

spotlights.name: The Delhi Durbar of 1911
spotlights.spot_it: Old photographs of a vast amphitheatre of tents and a domed pavilion where a crowned king and queen sit in purple robes.
spotlights.story_md: The 1911 Durbar was the only one attended by a reigning British monarch. **George V** and **Queen Mary** sat under a golden canopy on a field in north Delhi while about 100,000 people watched princes bow. The king wore a new **Imperial Crown of India**, made for the occasion with more than **6,000 diamonds**, because the law forbade the coronation crown from leaving Britain. At the end of the ceremony he announced the capital's move, a secret kept until that moment. The site, now **Coronation Park**, is a quiet field where statues of British kings and viceroys, removed from New Delhi's roundabouts after Independence, stand in a row.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It was the moment Delhi became a capital again.
spotlights.memory_hook: A secret, a crown, and statues that ended up in a field.

spotlights.name: Rashtrapati Bhavan
spotlights.spot_it: A long pale sandstone palace with a huge copper-coloured dome shaped like a Buddhist stupa, a tall column in its forecourt.
spotlights.story_md: Built as the **Viceroy's House**, it has about **340 rooms** and covers some 2 hectares under one roof, on a 130-hectare estate, making it one of the largest homes of any head of state. Lutyens blended classical columns with Indian forms: the dome echoes the **Sanchi stupa**, and the 'Delhi Order' columns carry carved stone bells, which, the story goes, can never ring, so the Raj would never end. The first Indian governor-general, **C. Rajagopalachari**, found it too grand and lived in a small set of rooms. The **Mughal Gardens** behind it, renamed **Amrit Udyan** in **2023**, open to the public each spring.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the most visible symbol of the Indian state.
spotlights.memory_hook: A stupa on a palace, built for a viceroy, lived in by a republic.

spotlights.name: Connaught Place
spotlights.spot_it: Two concentric rings of white colonnaded Georgian buildings around a circular park, with a giant tricolour flying in the centre.
spotlights.story_md: Designed by **Robert Tor Russell** and modelled on Bath's Royal Crescent, CP was the commercial heart of the new capital, named after the **Duke of Connaught**. Its inner and outer circles are now officially **Rajiv Chowk** and **Indira Chowk**, though nobody calls them that. Under the central park lies **Rajiv Chowk metro station**, one of the busiest in the network, and beside it **Palika Bazaar**, an underground market. In the mid-2010s CP was listed among the world's most expensive office locations by rent.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the meeting point of the city, above and below ground.
spotlights.memory_hook: Bath's crescent, bent into a circle, with a metro hub underneath.

spotlights.name: Jantar Mantar
spotlights.spot_it: Giant pink-and-white masonry instruments: a huge triangular sundial, curved quadrants and circular open-roofed structures.
spotlights.story_md: **Maharaja Jai Singh II** of Amber, a scholar of astronomy, built this observatory in **1724** with the permission of the Mughal emperor Muhammad Shah, the first of five he built (the biggest is in Jaipur). The **Samrat Yantra**, a 21 m triangular gnomon, is a giant equal-hour sundial. Jai Singh wanted better tables of planetary positions for calendars and astrology. Today the street outside is famous for something else: until 2017, Jantar Mantar was **Delhi's main protest site**, where farmers, ex-soldiers and activists camped, and Anna Hazare launched his 2011 anti-corruption fast.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It joins 18th-century Indian science and 21st-century Indian protest.
spotlights.memory_hook: A giant sundial that became a protest stage.

spotlights.name: The new Parliament House
spotlights.spot_it: A triangular sandstone building with a bronze national emblem on top, beside the old circular colonnaded Parliament.
spotlights.story_md: India's old Parliament, a **circular** building by Herbert Baker opened in 1927, was often compared to the **Chausath Yogini** temple at Mitaoli in Madhya Pradesh, though no record shows Baker used it. The new building, by architect **Bimal Patel**, is triangular and was built in about two and a half years. Its Lok Sabha seats **888** and its Rajya Sabha **384**, room for a joint session of **1,272**, planned for a future increase in seats after delimitation. Prime Minister Modi inaugurated it on **28 May 2023**, installing the **Sengol**, a gold-plated sceptre from Tamil Nadu, beside the Speaker's chair. The old building is now called **Samvidhan Sadan**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is where India's laws are now made, and a statement of how the state sees itself.
spotlights.memory_hook: From a circle to a triangle, with room for more MPs.

sections.title: The refugee city
sections.intro_md:
In 1941 Delhi had about **920,000** people. By 1951 it had about **1.74 million**. The difference was largely **Partition**. In the autumn of 1947, as Hindus and Sikhs fled west Punjab and Sindh, roughly **half a million refugees** poured into Delhi, while tens of thousands of its Muslims fled to Pakistan or were driven into camps at Purana Qila and Humayun's Tomb. The Muslim share of Delhi's population fell from about **33%** in 1941 to under **6%** in 1951. Old Delhi's character changed in months.

The new arrivals reshaped the city. The government built **colonies** for them, often named after leaders: **Lajpat Nagar**, **Rajinder Nagar**, **Patel Nagar**, **Malviya Nagar**, **Tilak Nagar**. Refugees opened shops on pavements that became markets. Punjabi food, Punjabi speech and Punjabi business culture became the city's mainstream. The grandparents' stories of 1947 still sit under many Delhi families.

Later waves built other neighbourhoods: Bengalis from East Pakistan in **Chittaranjan Park**, Tibetans after 1959 in **Majnu ka Tilla**, and from the 1970s on, migrants from Bihar, UP and the hills who now make up much of the workforce. Darker chapters belong here too: in **1984**, after Indira Gandhi's assassination, mobs killed about **2,800 Sikhs** in Delhi over three days.

spotlights.name: Lajpat Nagar
spotlights.spot_it: A packed market of salwar-suit shops, mehendi artists on the pavement and stalls of chole kulche, behind rows of three-storey houses.
spotlights.story_md: Lajpat Nagar was laid out around 1950 for families from west Punjab and the North-West Frontier, and named after the Punjabi nationalist **Lala Lajpat Rai**. Early residents got small plots or one-room tenements and turned their front rooms into shops. The **Central Market** grew from those stalls into one of Delhi's biggest bazaars for clothes, household goods and wedding shopping. Its success story, refugees with nothing who rebuilt a business in a generation, is repeated in family histories across Karol Bagh, Rajinder Nagar and Tilak Nagar.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how Partition's refugees remade Delhi's economy and culture.
spotlights.memory_hook: Lost everything in 1947, sold everything by 1960.

spotlights.name: Majnu ka Tilla
spotlights.spot_it: Narrow lanes strung with prayer flags, a Buddhist temple courtyard, monks in maroon robes and cafés selling laphing and thukpa.
spotlights.story_md: The name, 'Majnu's mound', comes from a 15th-century Sufi hermit nicknamed Majnu who ferried people across the Yamuna for free; **Guru Nanak** is said to have met him here, and a gurdwara marks the spot. In **1960** the government gave land beside it to refugees who had followed the **Dalai Lama** out of Tibet in 1959. The colony, officially **New Aruna Nagar**, became Delhi's 'Little Tibet', a hub for Tibetans travelling to Dharamsala and a favourite with Delhi University students for cheap momos and laphing, a cold, spicy mung-bean noodle.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is where two of Delhi's refugee stories, Sikh and Tibetan, sit side by side.
spotlights.memory_hook: A Sufi ferryman's mound became Little Tibet.

spotlights.name: Chittaranjan Park
spotlights.when: Founded in the 1960s for East Bengal displaced persons
spotlights.spot_it: Bengali signboards, a fish market with mustard-oil smells, and in October, giant Durga Puja pandals packed past midnight.
spotlights.story_md: Originally the **East Pakistan Displaced Persons' Colony**, CR Park was set up for Bengali government employees and families who had fled East Bengal after Partition. Plots were allotted from the 1960s. It is named after the nationalist lawyer **Chittaranjan Das**. Its **Kali Mandir** on a hillock and its four markets, especially **Market No. 1's** fish stalls, make it the centre of Delhi's Bengali life. During **Durga Puja**, pandals here draw crowds in the hundreds of thousands, and many Delhiites who are not Bengali make the trip for bhog and phuchka.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is Delhi's Bengal, and proof that the refugee city kept growing in many languages.
spotlights.memory_hook: A Kolkata neighbourhood on a south Delhi hillock.

sections.title: Many languages, every faith
sections.intro_md:
Delhi is where **Hindustani** was born. In the bazaars around the sultans' and Mughal camps, Persian, Turkic and Arabic words mixed with the local Khari Boli dialect; the word *Urdu* itself comes from the Turkic *ordu*, a camp. That same street speech, written in two scripts, became modern **Hindi** and **Urdu**.

Today Hindi is the main language for about **81%** of residents, followed by **Punjabi** (about 5%) and **Urdu** (about 6%) in the 2011 census. The **Delhi Official Languages Act, 2000** made Punjabi and Urdu the territory's second official languages, which is why metro signs and some government boards use them. Old Delhi's working-class Muslims still speak **Karkhandari**, a dialect of the artisans' workshops.

By religion, the 2011 census counted **81.7%** Hindus, **12.9%** Muslims, **3.4%** Sikhs, **1%** Jains and smaller numbers of Christians and Buddhists.

spotlights.name: Gurudwara Bangla Sahib
spotlights.spot_it: A white marble gurdwara with a gold onion dome, a large tank (sarovar) in front, and lines of people barefoot with heads covered.
spotlights.story_md: This was the bungalow of **Raja Jai Singh** of Amber, where the seven-year-old eighth Sikh Guru, **Har Krishan**, stayed in **1664** during an outbreak of smallpox and cholera. He served the sick with water from the well and caught smallpox himself, dying aged seven. The water of the **sarovar** is still considered healing. The **langar**, the free community kitchen, serves anyone who sits on the floor, usually **tens of thousands of meals a day**, cooked largely by volunteers. Its huge kitchens, with dal cooking in vats and machines turning out rotis, are open to visitors and anyone can join in.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the clearest example of Sikh seva in the capital.
spotlights.memory_hook: A boy guru, a healing well, free dal for all.

spotlights.name: Swaminarayan Akshardham
spotlights.spot_it: A huge, elaborately carved pink sandstone and white marble temple with a frieze of 148 stone elephants around its base.
spotlights.story_md: Built by the **BAPS Swaminarayan Sanstha** and opened in **2005**, the complex was put together by about **7,000 artisans** and some **300,000 volunteers** over five years. The central monument is carved from Rajasthani pink sandstone and Italian marble with no structural steel, in a traditional style the builders call **Maharu-Gurjara**. Its base, the **Gajendra Pith**, carries 148 life-size stone elephants. The complex also has a boat ride through a re-created history of India, a musical fountain, and a strict no-phones rule.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the most visited new monument in Delhi.
spotlights.memory_hook: Seven thousand carvers, 148 elephants, not a single steel beam.

spotlights.name: Lotus Temple
spotlights.spot_it: A white building of 27 marble-clad petals in groups of three, opening upward, on a raised platform with nine reflecting pools.
spotlights.story_md: The **Bahá'í House of Worship** was designed by the Iranian-born architect **Fariborz Sahba** and opened in **1986**. It has **27 free-standing petals** of white Greek marble arranged in clusters of three to form nine sides, as Bahá'í temples must. There are no idols, no sermons and no rituals: people of any faith sit in silence or listen to readings from many scriptures. It holds about **2,500** people. By some counts it has been among the most visited buildings in the world, drawing millions a year.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a modern landmark that belongs to no single faith.
spotlights.memory_hook: A marble lotus with no idols inside.

spotlights.name: The Jain bird hospital

where.label: Digambar Jain Lal Mandir, Chandni Chowk

spotlights.spot_it: A red sandstone Jain temple at the head of Chandni Chowk with a sign for the Charity Birds Hospital and cages of pigeons and parakeets.
spotlights.story_md: Opposite the Red Fort, the **Shri Digambar Jain Lal Mandir** is the oldest Jain temple in Delhi, its first version built in 1656 for Jain soldiers in the Mughal army. In **1929** the community added the **Charity Birds Hospital**, run on the Jain principle of **ahimsa**, non-harm to any living being. Vets treat thousands of injured birds a year, many pigeons cut by kite strings or hit by fans. Only vegetarian birds are admitted, it is said, though this is not strictly checked. Patients recover in cages on the upper floors, and on certain days the cured are released from the roof into the Old Delhi sky.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It turns a religious principle into daily, practical care.
spotlights.memory_hook: A Mughal-era temple runs an ICU for pigeons.

sections.title: What Delhi eats
sections.intro_md:
Delhi's food has three layers. The oldest is **Mughlai**, the meat cooking of the court and of Old Delhi's Muslim families: nihari, korma, kebabs and sheermal, best eaten in the lanes around Jama Masjid. The second is the **Bania and Kayastha** food of the old Hindu merchant families: chaat, kachori, parathas and sweets from Chandni Chowk's halwais. The third, and the loudest, is **Punjabi**: tandoori chicken, butter chicken, dal makhani, chole bhature, brought by Partition refugees and turned into the dining-out menu of all of India.

Newer layers keep arriving. **Momos**, brought by Tibetans and people from the hills and the northeast, are now sold at almost every market corner. Bihari litti, south Indian dosa and Bengali rolls have their own followings.

Delhi also argues about food in court. In **January 2024** the family that owns **Moti Mahal** sued the owners of the **Daryaganj** restaurant chain in the Delhi High Court over who invented butter chicken and dal makhani.

spotlights.name: Butter chicken
spotlights.spot_it: Pieces of charred tandoori chicken in a smooth, orange, buttery tomato gravy, finished with cream and kasuri methi.
spotlights.story_md: The standard story: at **Moti Mahal** in Peshawar and then in Daryaganj after 1947, cooks needed to use leftover tandoori chicken that dried out in the display. **Kundan Lal Gujral** is credited with tossing it into a sauce of tomatoes, butter and cream. Moti Mahal served Nehru, foreign heads of state and Jackie Kennedy. The **Daryaganj** chain, run by the family of **Kundan Lal Jaggi**, says Jaggi was Gujral's partner and a co-creator, citing a partnership deed from 1949. Moti Mahal's suit asked for **₹2 crore** in damages.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is Delhi's biggest food export to the world.
spotlights.memory_hook: Leftover chicken, a pot of butter, a court case.

spotlights.name: Paranthe Wali Gali
spotlights.spot_it: A narrow lane of tiny shops where parathas are deep-fried in ghee in iron kadhais, served on steel plates with three curries.
spotlights.story_md: Here parathas are not griddle-cooked but **deep-fried** in pure ghee, stuffed with anything from potato and paneer to **rabri, banana, karela, papad or lemon**. The oldest shops trace their family business to the **1870s**, run by Brahmin families, and the food is strictly vegetarian with no onion or garlic, suiting Jain and Vaishnav customers. The walls hold photographs of famous diners, from Jawaharlal Nehru and Indira Gandhi to film stars. The lane has shrunk from about 20 shops to a handful, as rents rise and children choose other careers.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It keeps a 150-year-old vegetarian tradition alive in the middle of Mughal Delhi.
spotlights.memory_hook: Parathas fried like puris, stuffed with banana.

spotlights.name: Karim's and nihari
spotlights.spot_it: A courtyard eatery in a lane by Jama Masjid, cauldrons of mutton curry, and plates of slow-cooked nihari glistening with fat.
spotlights.story_md: **Karim's** was opened in **1913** by **Haji Karimuddin**, whose family claims descent from cooks in the Mughal royal kitchens who fled after 1857. Its mutton korma, burra kebabs and stews drew everyone from rickshaw pullers to Bollywood. Old Delhi's greatest breakfast is **nihari**, beef or mutton shank cooked overnight in a sealed pot with a dark, spiced gravy and bone marrow, eaten before dawn with khamiri roti. The word comes from the Arabic *nahar*, morning, because it was meant to be eaten after the dawn prayer, and shops in the lanes can sell out by 8 am.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the living kitchen of Mughal Delhi.
spotlights.memory_hook: Cooked all night, eaten at dawn, sold out by breakfast.

spotlights.name: Daulat ki chaat
spotlights.spot_it: A vendor with a large tray of white foam, like a cloud, topped with saffron, khoya and silver leaf, sold by the spoonful.
spotlights.story_md: It looks like nothing and tastes like sweet air. Milk and cream are whipped by hand for hours, traditionally left out under the **winter night sky** so dew can set the froth, and served before the sun melts it. It is topped with sugar, saffron, pistachio and silver leaf. The name, 'wealth's snack', may refer to how fleeting both are. You can only find it in winter in Old Delhi; the same dessert is called **malaiyyo** in Varanasi and **makhan malai** in Lucknow. Vendors stop by about noon, because the foam collapses in warm air.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a dessert you can only eat in one season, in one neighbourhood.
spotlights.memory_hook: Made with dew, killed by sunshine.

spotlights.name: Chole bhature
spotlights.when: Punjabi, popular in Delhi from the 1940s
spotlights.spot_it: Two huge puffed, golden, fried breads beside a dark, tangy chickpea curry, sliced onions, pickle and a green chilli.
spotlights.story_md: A heavy breakfast that Delhi eats at lunch. The **chole** are cooked dark with tea leaves or dried amla and spiced with anardana; the **bhatura** is a fermented, deep-fried bread that should balloon in the oil. The dish came with Punjabi refugees, and famous stalls such as **Sita Ram Diwan Chand** in Paharganj, started by a refugee in 1950, built empires on it. Delhiites argue fiercely over which shop, which neighbourhood and which accompaniment is best, often in the same conversation where they swear they are dieting.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the taste of the Punjabi Delhi that Partition made.
spotlights.memory_hook: A bread that balloons, a curry made dark with tea.

sections.title: Festivals, kites and the oldest street theatre
sections.intro_md:
Delhi's calendar is crowded because every community that arrived brought its festivals. **Diwali** in October or November is the biggest, followed closely by **Dussehra**, when hundreds of neighbourhood stages perform the **Ramlila** and giant effigies of Ravana burn. **Eid** fills the Jama Masjid and its lanes, **Gurpurab** fills the gurdwaras, **Durga Puja** fills CR Park and **Chhath** fills the Yamuna ghats with migrants from Bihar and eastern UP.

Some traditions are purely Delhi's own. On **Independence Day**, the sky over Old Delhi fills with kites, a custom of kite battles that goes back to the Mughals. In autumn, **Phool Walon Ki Sair** in Mehrauli carries flower fans to a Hindu temple and a Sufi shrine. The capital also holds the national parades: the **Republic Day** parade on Kartavya Path on 26 January, and **Beating Retreat** at Vijay Chowk three days later.

Music has deep roots here. The **Delhi gharana** of tabla, founded by **Siddhar Khan** in the 18th century, is usually counted as the oldest tabla school.

spotlights.name: Phool Walon Ki Sair
spotlights.spot_it: A procession carrying huge fans (pankhas) made of flowers to Yogmaya temple and the shrine of Bakhtiyar Kaki, with shehnai and dancers.
spotlights.story_md: In **1812** the British exiled **Mirza Jahangir**, a son of the Mughal emperor Akbar II, to Allahabad for firing at the British Resident. His mother vowed that if he returned she would offer a chadar of flowers at the Sufi shrine of **Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki** in Mehrauli. He did, and the whole city joined her procession, adding a flower fan for the Hindu **Yogmaya temple** next door. The festival, 'procession of the florists', ran yearly until the British banned it in **1942** under 'divide and rule'. **Nehru** helped revive it in **1961**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a living symbol of Hindu Muslim togetherness in Delhi.
spotlights.memory_hook: A mother's vow, two shrines, one flower fan.

spotlights.name: Delhi's Ramlila
spotlights.spot_it: A lit stage in a park with actors in glittering crowns and painted faces, a crowd on plastic chairs, and a towering paper Ravana waiting to burn.
spotlights.story_md: The Ramlila retells the Ramayana over about ten nights before **Dussehra**. UNESCO inscribed the **Ramlila** tradition on its intangible heritage list in **2008**. Delhi's big shows, such as **Lav Kush Ramlila** at Red Fort grounds, now cast television and film stars and draw politicians, while hundreds of small neighbourhood ones use local actors. The finale burns effigies of **Ravana**, **Meghnad** and **Kumbhkaran** stuffed with firecrackers; some are more than **30 m** tall. The effigy makers of **Titarpur** in west Delhi build thousands each year from bamboo, paper and glue, in a market that fills whole streets in September.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the most widely attended theatre in Delhi.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ten nights of epic, one night of fire.

spotlights.name: Independence Day kite battles
spotlights.spot_it: A sky over the old city filled with hundreds of small paper kites, people shouting 'bo kaata' from every rooftop.
spotlights.story_md: On **15 August**, while the prime minister speaks from the Red Fort, Old Delhi takes to its roofs. Kite flying in Delhi goes back to Mughal pastimes, and the 15 August custom is often explained as a celebration of freedom. The game is to cut rival kites: the winning flyer shouts **'bo kaata!'**. Glass-coated **manja**, and especially Chinese nylon manja, cuts deep, killing birds and injuring motorcyclists, so the Delhi government and the **National Green Tribunal** have banned nylon and glass-coated string since **2016**. Pigeon fanciers on the same rooftops wave flags to bring their flocks home.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is how the old city celebrates the nation's birthday, in its own way.
spotlights.memory_hook: The PM speaks, the rooftops shout 'bo kaata'.

spotlights.name: Chhath on the Yamuna

where.label: Yamuna ghats, ITO and Kalindi Kunj

spotlights.spot_it: Women in bright saris standing waist-deep in the river at sunset, holding bamboo baskets of fruit and lamps up to the sun.
spotlights.story_md: Chhath, a festival of the sun god from **Bihar and eastern UP**, has become one of Delhi's biggest public festivals as **Purvanchali** migrants grew to an estimated quarter or more of the city's voters. Devotees fast for about **36 hours** without water and offer *arghya* to the setting and rising sun from the water. In recent years images of women standing in the Yamuna's **toxic white foam** have become a national symbol of the river's pollution. In **2025** the Delhi government promised a clean river for Chhath and built special ghats.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how migration reshapes a city's public calendar.
spotlights.memory_hook: Prayers to the sun, waist-deep in foam.

sections.title: How Delhi moves and lives
sections.intro_md:
Delhi is a city of long distances and sharp divides. Its planned colonies, unauthorised colonies, urban villages, slums and Lutyens' bungalows can sit within a kilometre of one another. About **4 million** people live in some **1,700 unauthorised colonies**, built on farmland without approved plans; a 2019 law began giving them ownership rights.

Getting around has changed more than anything. The **Delhi Metro**, opened in **2002**, now carries several million trips a day. Buses moved to compressed natural gas in the early 2000s after a **Supreme Court** order, and in the 2020s the city built one of the largest electric bus fleets in India. Women travel free on DTC buses since **2019**.

Society runs on certain constants. Wedding season, roughly November to February, closes roads with baraats and brass bands. Delhi's **Resident Welfare Associations** run colony life, from security guards to park maintenance. And a stereotype, Delhiites as aggressive drivers and status-conscious show-offs, is popular in the rest of India; road crash data does show Delhi among the highest totals of road deaths among Indian cities.

spotlights.name: Delhi Metro
spotlights.spot_it: Steel trains on elevated concrete tracks above traffic, colour-coded lines, women-only first coaches, and tokens shaped like coins.
spotlights.story_md: Built by the **Delhi Metro Rail Corporation** under **E. Sreedharan**, the 'Metro Man', the first stretch opened on **24 December 2002**. Today DMRC's own network runs to roughly **375 km** on 10 colour-coded lines with about **270 stations**, and more than 400 km counting connected lines in Noida and Gurugram, among the longest systems in the world. The first carriage of every train is **reserved for women**. In 2011 Delhi Metro became the first railway project to earn **carbon credits** from the UN for cutting emissions.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It changed how a city of 20 million moves, and how its women travel.
spotlights.memory_hook: Opened on Christmas Eve, now one of the longest metros on Earth.

spotlights.name: Green-and-yellow CNG autos
spotlights.spot_it: A three-wheeled rickshaw in green and yellow, a meter that is rarely used, and a driver negotiating the fare out of the window.
spotlights.story_md: In **1998**, in the case **M. C. Mehta v. Union of India**, the Supreme Court ordered Delhi's entire public transport fleet, buses, autos and taxis, to switch to **compressed natural gas**. The deadline slipped and operators protested, but by **2002** Delhi had one of the largest CNG fleets on the planet. The green-and-yellow paint marks a CNG auto; black-and-yellow marks a CNG taxi. The air improved for a few years, until vehicle numbers exploded. Delhi now has well over **90,000** autos, and **e-rickshaws**, battery tuk-tuks, have spread to almost every metro station since the 2010s.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It was the world's biggest switch of a public fleet to gas, forced by judges.
spotlights.memory_hook: The Supreme Court painted the autos green.

sections.title: How Delhi earns
sections.intro_md:
Delhi's economy is a services machine. In **2025 to 26**, services made up about **86%** of its value added, industry about **13%** and farming under **1%**. Its GSDP was projected at about **₹13.27 lakh crore** at current prices, growing **9.4%** in that year. Government, finance, trade, real estate, IT, hotels and the vast business of being the capital all feed it.

It is also India's biggest **wholesale** market. Old Delhi's specialised bazaars, many dating to Mughal times, sell to traders from across north India: spices at **Khari Baoli**, textiles at **Chandni Chowk** and **Gandhi Nagar**, paper at **Chawri Bazar**, hardware at **Bhagirath Palace**, which is one of Asia's biggest electrical markets. **Azadpur Mandi** feeds much of north India with fruit and vegetables.

The flip side: a large share of workers are informal, and the wider NCR, not Delhi itself, now holds most of the new offices and factories, in **Gurugram** and **Noida**.

spotlights.name: Khari Baoli
spotlights.spot_it: A crowded street of sacks of red chillies, turmeric, dried fruit and whole spices, porters with loads on their heads, and sneezing visitors.
spotlights.story_md: **Khari Baoli**, 'salty step-well', is named after a step-well of salty water dug in the 16th century that has since vanished. It is often called **Asia's largest wholesale spice market**. Traders sell spices, nuts, dried fruit, herbs and rice by the tonne. The **Gadodia Market**, a 1920s building with a central courtyard, is at its heart. A rooftop walk above it gives one of the best views of Old Delhi. Breathing here is an adventure: the chilli dust is enough to make visitors cough in the lanes, and porters cover their faces.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is how the spices of half of India reach kitchens across the north.
spotlights.memory_hook: A salty well disappeared, and the spices stayed.

spotlights.name: Nehru Place
spotlights.spot_it: Grey concrete office blocks around a crowded plaza of stalls selling laptops, cables, printer ink and software.
spotlights.story_md: Planned as a **district centre** in the 1970s, Nehru Place became the hub of north India's **computer hardware** trade. Its stalls sell everything from new laptops to second-hand parts, repairs while you wait, and custom-built gaming PCs. For years it was also notorious for **pirated software**; the US trade representative listed it among the world's 'notorious markets' for counterfeits in the 2010s. Behind the stalls are the offices of companies, startups and IT firms.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the hands-on base of Delhi's tech economy.
spotlights.memory_hook: Fix your laptop in an hour, under a concrete sky.

sections.title: Smog, foam and a gasping city
sections.intro_md:
Every **November**, Delhi becomes international news for one reason: its air. As winds drop and temperatures fall, a lid of cold air traps pollution near the ground. Smoke from **crop-residue burning** in Punjab and Haryana, vehicle exhaust, construction dust, industry, waste fires and Diwali firecrackers pile in. The **Air Quality Index** regularly exceeds **400**, the 'severe' band, and in bad weeks crosses **500**. In mid-**December 2025** readings above **600** pushed the city into **GRAP Stage 4**, the strictest emergency curbs.

The health cost is real. Studies link Delhi's air to shorter lives; the University of Chicago's Air Quality Life Index has estimated that meeting WHO guidelines would add more than **ten years** to the average Delhiite's life expectancy. Schools close, flights are delayed, and doctors see a wave of respiratory illness.

Water is the other crisis. Delhi depends on the Yamuna, the Ganga canal and groundwater, while summers bring shortages in poorer colonies served by tankers.

spotlights.name: Delhi's winter smog

where.label: Whole city, worst from late October to January

spotlights.spot_it: A thick grey-yellow haze that hides buildings a few hundred metres away, the sun a dull orange disc, and masks on every face.
spotlights.story_md: **PM2.5**, particles smaller than 2.5 microns, is the main killer. On bad days in November, levels have reached **over 30 times** the WHO's 24-hour guideline. In **November 2017**, United Airlines briefly suspended flights to Delhi; in **2019** the government declared a public health emergency and handed out masks to schoolchildren. Responses include the **Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP)**, odd-even car rationing trials in 2016 and 2019, two experimental **smog towers** in 2021, and bans on firecrackers that are widely ignored.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of the biggest public health problems in any city on Earth.
spotlights.memory_hook: Breathe in, and you have smoked a few cigarettes.

spotlights.name: Toxic foam on the Yamuna
spotlights.when: Every autumn, worst October to November
spotlights.spot_it: Piles of white froth floating on the river like snowbanks, sometimes metres high, near the Okhla barrage.
spotlights.story_md: The foam is not natural. It forms when **phosphates and surfactants** from detergents in untreated sewage, along with industrial effluents, get churned at the **Okhla barrage**. Low river flow after the monsoon makes it worse. It often peaks just as devotees enter the river for **Chhath**. In **2025** the new government launched a **45-point action plan** to clean the river, promising to stop untreated sewage reaching it, rebuild sewage treatment plants and make the river clean by **December 2027**. In 2025 the chief minister said 22 of Delhi's 38 sewage treatment plants were not meeting standards.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the most visible sign that Delhi's sewage goes straight into its river.
spotlights.memory_hook: Detergent bubbles, three metres high, on a holy river.

sections.title: People to know
sections.intro_md:
Delhi has produced or adopted a long list of rulers, poets and saints, many already met today: Razia, Khusrau, Nizamuddin, Ghalib, Zafar. The modern list is long too, partly because so many people arrive here to make a career. A few are true Delhi products.

**Khushwant Singh**, the novelist and columnist whose father built much of New Delhi, wrote *Delhi: A Novel* and *Train to Pakistan*. **Amrita Sher-Gil**'s last studio was in Lahore, but Delhi's National Gallery of Modern Art holds most of her paintings. The city has made cricketers, politicians, film stars and designers.

Three modern figures stand out, chosen because each changed the national idea of what Delhi is: a chief minister who rebuilt the city's infrastructure, a cricketer who made West Delhi aggression a style, and a film star who left a Delhi middle-class home to become one of the most famous actors on Earth.

spotlights.name: Sheila Dikshit
spotlights.spot_it: A silver-haired woman in a crisp cotton sari, often at a podium with a flyover or a metro line in the background.
spotlights.story_md: Sheila Dikshit was **Delhi's longest-serving chief minister**, three terms over **15 years** for the Congress. Her years saw the city's biggest infrastructure push: dozens of flyovers, the first metro lines, CNG buses, the shift of polluting industries out of residential areas, and greener roadsides. She also presided over the **2010 Commonwealth Games**, whose preparation became a byword for delays and corruption allegations, though she was not charged. She lost her own seat to **Arvind Kejriwal** in 2013 in one of India's great political upsets, and died in 2019.
spotlights.why_it_matters: She shaped the modern city that many Delhiites live in today.
spotlights.memory_hook: Fifteen years, a hundred flyovers, one upset.

spotlights.name: Virat Kohli
spotlights.spot_it: A bearded batsman with a fierce glare and a tattooed arm, celebrating a century with a roar.
spotlights.story_md: Kohli grew up in **Uttam Nagar** and **Paschim Vihar** and trained at the **West Delhi Cricket Academy** under **Rajkumar Sharma**. In **December 2006**, aged 18, he batted for Delhi in a Ranji match the morning after his father's death, scored 90 and then went to the cremation. He led India to the Under-19 World Cup in **2008**. He has scored more than **80 international centuries**, second only to Sachin Tendulkar, and holds the record for most ODI hundreds. He retired from T20 internationals after India's **2024** World Cup win and from Tests in **May 2025**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He made a West Delhi street swagger into a national style.
spotlights.memory_hook: Batted on the morning of his father's death, and kept batting for two decades.

spotlights.name: Shah Rukh Khan
spotlights.spot_it: A dark-haired actor with dimples and outstretched arms, the signature pose from his romantic films.
spotlights.story_md: Born in New Delhi to a family that had migrated from Peshawar, **Shah Rukh Khan** studied at **St Columba's School** and **Hansraj College**, and acted in Delhi theatre with **Barry John**. He moved to Bombay in **1991** after his mother's death, and within a few years became the biggest star in Hindi cinema. He is among the richest actors in the world, and his films are watched across South Asia, the Middle East and the diaspora. In **2025** he received his first **National Film Award** for best actor, for *Jawan*, after more than three decades in film.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He is the biggest example of a Delhi middle-class boy conquering a national industry.
spotlights.memory_hook: A Delhi theatre kid became the King of Bollywood.

sections.title: Places that surprise Delhiites too
sections.intro_md:
Delhi has three UNESCO World Heritage Sites, the Qutb complex, Humayun's Tomb and the Red Fort, and more than **170 monuments** protected by the Archaeological Survey of India, plus over a thousand listed heritage buildings. Many of the best are not famous.

The city's ruins are scattered everywhere: in the middle of roundabouts, beside parking lots, inside housing colonies, in the middle of Lodhi Garden and in the **Mehrauli Archaeological Park**, where more than **100** monuments stand in about 80 hectares of scrub. Restoration since the 2000s has also produced new green spaces, especially **Sunder Nursery**, restored by the Aga Khan Trust for Culture.

These three places reward the curious: a step-well in the middle of office blocks, a Mughal nursery turned park, and a 16th-century tomb that keeps a secret about a poet and a man named Kamali.

spotlights.name: Agrasen ki Baoli
spotlights.spot_it: A long, narrow stone step-well with 103 steps descending between arched walls, hidden among office towers.
spotlights.story_md: Agrasen ki Baoli is a **60 m long**, **15 m wide** stepped well whose **103 steps** lead down to a water level that has mostly dried up. Tradition credits the legendary king **Agrasen**, ancestor of the Agrawal community, but the present structure is thought to date from the Tughlaq or Lodi period. It was nearly forgotten until films and Instagram rediscovered it: *PK* (2014) and *Sultan* (2016) were shot here. Urban legends about haunting and dark water drawing people in made it a favourite for ghost-hunting students.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a reminder that Delhi once stored rainwater in public architecture.
spotlights.memory_hook: A hundred steps down, into the 14th century, five minutes from CP.

spotlights.name: Sunder Nursery
spotlights.spot_it: A formal park of axial water channels and lawns, with restored Mughal tombs, a lotus pond and a bonsai house.
spotlights.story_md: This 36-hectare garden was a Mughal grove, then a British nursery that raised trees for New Delhi's avenues from about **1913**. The Aga Khan Trust for Culture restored it over about a decade, rebuilding **15 monuments**, including the **Sunderwala Burj** and **Lakkarwala Burj**, and planting some **300 species** of trees. It opened to the public in **2018**. With its mughal-style axes and bird life, it became Delhi's favourite new park, a weekend venue for food markets and picnics.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how restoration can create new public space in a crowded city.
spotlights.memory_hook: A nursery for New Delhi's trees became a park of its own.

sections.title: Delhi now: 2025 to 2026
sections.intro_md:
**February 2025**: the BJP won **48 of 70** seats in the Delhi assembly election, ending the Aam Aadmi Party's ten years in power and returning the BJP after **27 years**. Arvind Kejriwal lost his own New Delhi seat. On **20 February 2025** **Rekha Gupta**, a first-time MLA from Shalimar Bagh, was sworn in at Ramlila Maidan as Delhi's fourth woman chief minister.

**October 2025**: IIT Kanpur ran Delhi's first **cloud-seeding** trials to wash out smog. Clouds had only about 15 to 20% moisture and no measurable rain fell; the IIT director called it not fully successful. **10 November 2025**: a car bomb exploded near the Red Fort metro station during evening traffic. The NIA's chargesheet in September 2026 put the toll at 11 dead and 29 injured. **December 2025**: AQI readings above 600 triggered GRAP Stage 4; the territory was reorganised into **13 districts**.

**March 2026**: the Economic Survey estimated per capita income at **₹5,31,610**, and the government presented a **₹1,03,700 crore** budget for 2026 to 27. In mid-2026, new **Metro Phase 4** sections continued to open, and the Yamuna clean-up faced its first deadlines.

spotlights.name: Rekha Gupta
spotlights.spot_it: A woman in a sari with a saffron stole at a podium, the BJP lotus behind her.
spotlights.story_md: Rekha Gupta, born in **1974**, started in student politics with the ABVP and was president of the **Delhi University Students' Union** in 1996 to 97. She served three terms as a municipal councillor before winning **Shalimar Bagh** in **2025** by about 29,000 votes, her first assembly win. She became Delhi's **fourth woman chief minister**, after Sushma Swaraj, Sheila Dikshit and Atishi. Her government's agenda includes the Yamuna clean-up, a ₹2,500-a-month scheme for women promised in the campaign, Ayushman Bharat health cover for Delhi, and pollution measures including the cloud-seeding trial.
spotlights.why_it_matters: She leads the first BJP government in Delhi since 1998.
spotlights.memory_hook: From the student union to the Secretariat.

spotlights.name: Bharat Mandapam
spotlights.spot_it: A vast curving convention centre shaped like a conch shell, with a giant bronze Nataraja statue at its entrance.
spotlights.story_md: Built on the site of the old **Pragati Maidan** exhibition halls, including the much-loved 1972 **Hall of Nations** demolished in 2017 despite architects' protests, **Bharat Mandapam** opened in **July 2023**. Its shape is said to be inspired by the **shankh**, the conch shell. It hosted the **G20 summit** of **September 2023**, where the African Union joined as a permanent member. At its entrance stands a **27-foot** Nataraja statue made by sculptors of Swamimalai in Tamil Nadu, said to be the world's tallest.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the stage on which India now hosts the world.
spotlights.memory_hook: A conch-shaped hall, a 27-foot dancing Shiva, and the G20.

sections.title: Myths, half-truths and the recap
sections.intro_md:
Delhi carries a load of stories that are repeated so often they sound like history. Some are true, some half true and some false. Here are the commonest.

**Myth: Delhi has exactly seven cities.** The number is a tradition. Historians count anywhere from seven to fifteen, depending on whether you count Lal Kot and Qila Rai Pithora separately, include Mubarakabad or the Mughal suburbs, or add New Delhi.

**Myth: Butter chicken was invented by one man in Daryaganj.** Two families claim it, the case is in court, and the dish's real origin story is a blend of kitchen accident and marketing.

**Half-truth: The Iron Pillar never rusts.** It does rust, slowly. A thin protective layer, helped by its phosphorus content and dry air, keeps the rust from eating in.

**False: Indraprastha's ruins have been found at Purana Qila.** Excavations found Painted Grey Ware from roughly the epic period, but nothing proves the epic's city was there.

**Recap:** Delhi is a city of layers. Rock and river, sultans and Mughals, a British capital, a refugee city and a global megacity, all in 1,484 square kilometres, with a stubborn talent for surviving its own destructions.

best_facts.fact: The Iron Pillar in the Qutb complex was cast about 1,600 years ago and has stood in the open ever since with barely any rust; scientists traced the secret to unusually high phosphorus that lets a protective film form.

best_facts.fact: Delhi's black kites thrive partly because people in Old Delhi throw meat into the air for them as charity, giving the city one of the densest populations of large raptors of any city on Earth.

best_facts.fact: In 1356 Firoz Shah Tughlaq moved a 13 m Ashokan pillar 200 km to Delhi on a 42-wheeled cart and by river, though nobody at his court could read it; the script was deciphered only in 1837.

best_facts.fact: Every Thursday people leave written letters to djinns in the ruins of Feroz Shah Kotla, asking for jobs, cures and love.
best_facts.why_surprising: A 14th-century ruin works as a post office for spirits.

best_facts.fact: Humayun, the second Mughal emperor, died after falling down the steep stairs of his own library in the Purana Qila in 1556.
best_facts.why_surprising: An emperor who won back an empire was undone by a staircase.

best_facts.fact: Two Delhi restaurant families are fighting in the Delhi High Court over who invented butter chicken and dal makhani, with ₹2 crore in damages claimed.
best_facts.why_surprising: A curry is the subject of an intellectual property suit.

best_facts.fact: Daulat ki chaat, an Old Delhi winter dessert, is hand-whipped milk foam traditionally set by night dew and sold only until the sun melts it.

best_facts.why_surprising: Judges, not ministers, repainted the city's autos.

best_facts.fact: A Jain temple opposite the Red Fort has run a hospital for birds since 1929.
best_facts.why_surprising: A Mughal-era temple keeps an ICU for pigeons.

best_facts.fact: Delhi covers about 2% of the Yamuna's length but is estimated to contribute about 76% of its pollution load.
best_facts.why_surprising: A tiny stretch does most of the damage.

best_facts.fact: Bahadur Shah Zafar, the last Mughal emperor, was exiled to Rangoon and buried in an unmarked grave that was found only in 1991.

side_dish.title: Why the Iron Pillar does not rust
side_dish.body_md:
Rust is iron trying to go back to being rock. Iron, water and oxygen react to form hydrated iron oxides, the flaky orange stuff, and because ordinary rust is porous and falls off, fresh metal is always exposed to the next attack. A steel bar left outside in a wet city can be eaten through in decades.

The Iron Pillar does something different. The Indian metallurgist **R. Balasubramaniam** of IIT Kanpur studied it for years and published the clearest explanation in the journal *Corrosion Science* in 2000 and in later papers. The pillar's wrought iron contains about **0.1% phosphorus**, far more than modern steel, and very little sulphur. As the surface corrodes, the phosphorus helps form a thin, dense layer that includes a compound called **misawite** and iron hydrogen phosphate. This layer sticks to the metal and blocks oxygen and water from getting through. It is a self-repairing shield.

Two other things help. The smiths did not melt the iron fully; they forge-welded lumps of it, leaving bits of slag inside that also influence how the surface reacts. And Delhi's climate is dry for much of the year, so the surface is wet for only part of the time.

Modern engineers use the same idea. **Weathering steel**, often sold as Corten, is designed to grow a stable, dark rust skin that protects what is underneath. Look at old railway bridges or modern sculptures with a deep brown surface and you are seeing the pillar's trick at work.

offline_task.title: Make a quick Delhi-style chole
offline_task.body_md:
Chole is the Punjabi-Delhi dish you can make tonight without a tandoor.

**Serves 2:** use one can of chickpeas or a cup of soaked and boiled ones. If you have a tea bag, boil the chickpeas with it for 10 minutes for that dark Delhi colour, then remove it. Heat 2 tablespoons of oil, add a teaspoon of cumin, then 1 finely chopped onion, and fry until deep brown. Add a tablespoon of ginger-garlic paste, then 2 chopped tomatoes, half a teaspoon of turmeric, a teaspoon of chilli powder, a teaspoon of coriander powder and salt. Cook until the oil separates. Add the chickpeas with a cup of water and simmer for 15 minutes, mashing a few to thicken. Finish with a teaspoon of chana masala or garam masala and a squeeze of lemon, or a teaspoon of dried pomegranate seed powder (anardana) if you have it.

Serve with bhature if you are brave, or with rotis, sliced onion, green chilli and pickle. While it simmers, think of the Partition refugees who sold this dish from pavement stalls and built businesses on it.
